result: Mass spectrometry analysis identified oxidized Trp residues in PSII core proteins from Arabidopsis wild-type and var2 mutant (lacking FtsH2), with increased oxidation levels of Trp-14 and Trp-317 in D1 in the var2 mutant. Multiple oxidized Trp residues were also identified in Chlamydomonas PSII, with most located on the lumenal side surrounding the Mn4O5Ca cluster, while Trp-14 in D1 and Trp-21 in D2 are located on the stromal side.
evaluation: Reviewers 3 and 4 explicitly acknowledge the mass spectrometry data as solid evidence. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'find that FtsH mutants of Arabidopsis have increased OPTM, especially the formation of NFK at multiple Trp residues of D1 including the W14' as a strength. Reviewer 4 notes the mass spectrometry approach provides evidence that 'Trp oxidation (in particular the oxidation of Trp14) in coordination with FtsH results in the degradation of D1 protein.' However, Reviewer 3 notes a weakness: 'It is unclear why the level of Trp oxidation was not analyzed in the Chlamydomonas ftsH 1-1 mutant as done for the var 2 mutant.'

result: Site-directed mutagenesis in Chlamydomonas showed that Trp-14 and Trp-317 substitution to Ala impaired growth and reduced PSII protein accumulation, while Phe substitution had little effect under growth light but W14F exhibited significantly impaired growth under high light, with W14F having more profound effects than W317F on the PSII repair cycle.
evaluation: Reviewers generally accept these phenotypic data. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'a site-directed mutation of W14 to phenylalanine (W14F), mimicking NFK, results in accelerated D1 degradation in Chlamydomonas' as a strength. Reviewer 4 confirms 'the author's use site-directed mutagenesis of Trp residues undergoing OPTM in the D1 protein coupled with their D1 degradation assays (Figure 3 and 4), provides evidence that Trp oxidation (in particular the oxidation of Trp14) in coordination with FtsH results in the degradation of D1 protein.'

result: D1 degradation assays under growth and high light conditions with and without chloramphenicol (CAM) showed that W14F and W14F/W317F exhibited enhanced D1 degradation under high light compared to control and W317F, while PSII activity declined at similar rates in all lines, indicating equal photodamage but enhanced proteolytic degradation in W14F mutants.
evaluation: This result receives mixed evaluation. Reviewer 2 raises a fundamental concern: 'Stability or activity (Fv/Fm) was not affected in PSII with the W14F mutation in D1. If W14F really represents the status of PSII with oxidized D1, what is the reason for the degradation of almost normal D1?' Reviewer 3 identifies a critical reproducibility issue: 'The D1 degradation assay seems not repeatable for the W14F mutant. High light minus CAM results in Fig. 3 shows a statistically significant decrease in D1 levels for W14F at multiple time points but the same assay in Fig. 4a does not produce a statistically significant decrease at 90 min of incubation.' Reviewer 2 also suggests 'high light may induce another event which is recognized by FtsH. The W14F is just an enhancer' rather than a direct mimic of oxidation.

result: Pulse-labeling experiments demonstrated that D1 synthesis proceeded comparably in all Trp-substituted lines and control, indicating that Trp-14 substitution to Phe enhanced D1 degradation without affecting D1 synthesis, light-induced PSII damage, or PSII stability.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this data as supporting evidence that the W14F effect is specific to degradation. Reviewer 4 notes 'W14F affected neither D1 synthesis (Figure 5), stability of PSII complex formation, nor PSII activity under non-photoinhibitory conditions' as part of the compelling evidence. No reviewer challenges the synthesis data directly.

result: CP43 Trp mutants (W353A, W375A, W353F, W375F) showed that only W353A/W375A double mutant had severely reduced D1 and CP43 levels, while W353F showed only slight growth reduction under high light, leading to the conclusion that Trp oxidation in CP43 has little impact on PSII repair.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this negative result. Reviewer 3 notes 'None of Trp substitutions at the site of OPTM in CP43 (Trp-353 and Trp-375) affected the D1 degradation' and 'the CP43 transformants did not show the increased photosensitivity' but points out a discrepancy: 'the authors write that CP43 mutant W353F has no growth phenotype under high light but Figure S6 reveals otherwise. The slow growth of this mutant is in line with the earlier observation made by Anderson et al., 2002.' Reviewer 4 confirms 'Trp oxidation in CP43 appeared to have little impact on the PSII repair (Supplemental Figure S6).'

result: Genetic analysis using ftsh1-1 mutant background showed that the enhanced D1 degradation in W14F and W14F/W317F was partially mitigated in the ftsh1-1 background, demonstrating that FtsH plays a key role in the increased D1 degradation in these mutants.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this genetic evidence. Reviewer 3 explicitly lists as a strength: 'accelerated D1 degradation of W14F mutant is mitigated in an ftsH1 mutant background of Chlamydomonas.' Reviewer 4 states 'their D1 degradation assays coupled with the use of a ftsh mutant provide further significant support that Trp14 oxidation and FtsH activity are strongly linked.'

result: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that D1 Trp-14 forms a hydrogen bond with PsbI Ser-25 in wild-type, and this bond is disrupted when Trp-14 is oxidized to NFK or replaced with Phe, leading to increased structural fluctuation of the D1 N-terminal tail, with W14F showing similar trends to oxidized Trp-14.
evaluation: Reviewers have mixed views on the simulation data. Reviewer 2 questions the validity: 'To focus on the PSII in which W14 is oxidized, this research depends on the W14F mutant lines. It is critical how exactly the W-to-F substitution mimics the oxidized W. The authors tried to show it in Figure 5. Because of the technical difficulty, it may be unfair to request more evidence. But the paper would be more convincing with the results directly monitoring the oxidized D1 to be recognized by FtsH.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges it as a strength: 'Authors raise an intriguing possibility that the OPTM disrupts the hydrogen bonding between W14 residue of D1 and the serine 25 (S25) of PsbI...This is an interesting hypothesis and the authors provide some molecular dynamics simulation data in support of this.' However, Reviewer 3 also suggests 'Can this hypothesis be further tested by replacing the S25 of PsbI with Ala, for example?'

result: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed that the relative D1 protein amount was statistically higher in W14F/W317F than control in FtsH-immunoprecipitated samples, indicating that W14F increased affinity between FtsH and reaction center proteins, leading to enhanced D1 degradation.
evaluation: Reviewers raise concerns about this data. Reviewer 3 notes multiple issues: 'It is also unclear to me what is the rationale for showing D1-FtsH interaction data only for the double mutant but not for the single mutant (W14F). Why is the FtsH pulldown of D2 not statistically significant (p value ≤0.1). Wouldn't one expect FtsH pulls down the RC47 complex containing D1, D2, and RC47. Probing the RC47 level would have been useful in settling this.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges it as supporting evidence but questions the interpretation and completeness.

result: The study's main conclusion that oxidative post-translational modification of Trp-14 at the N-terminus of D1 is correlated with D1 degradation by FtsH during high-light stress, with Trp-14 oxidation being one of the key OPTMs for degrading photodamaged D1 and triggering enhanced FtsH access for processive degradation.
evaluation: The main conclusion receives mixed evaluation. The Editor/Reviewer 1 states 'The evidence supporting the authors' conclusions is solid.' Reviewer 4 calls the data and arguments 'very compelling.' However, Reviewer 2 suggests an alternative interpretation: 'W14F mutation partially modifies the structure of D1 under high light and this structural modification of D1 is sensed by FtsH. Namely, high light may induce another event which is recognized by FtsH. The W14F is just an enhancer.' Reviewer 3 states 'A rigorous demonstration of OPTM as a marker for D1 degradation is yet to be made in my opinion' and notes 'some of the data are correlative and do not provide mechanistic insight.' Reviewer 3 also points out: 'The rationale for analyzing a single oxidative modification (W14) as a D1 degradation signal is unclear. D1 N-terminus is modified at multiple sites.'
